status: word-specific content authored; final candidate verification required

words.definition: A defined group of organisms of one species in a stated place and time; its boundary includes the individuals being counted or studied.

structure.text: Population is the group noun; population-level distinguishes group measurements from an individual's characteristics.

words.whatItDoes: A stated boundary determines which births, deaths and movements enter the count.
words.commonConfusion: A community includes multiple species, unlike one population.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why must place and time be stated before comparing two population counts?

words.definition: All allele copies at all loci in a defined population.

structure.text: Pool is a collection metaphor; gene identifies the inherited variants being considered.

words.whatItDoes: Allele copies enter frequency calculations across the defined population.
words.commonConfusion: A gene pool is not one individual's genotype.
words.retrievalPrompt: How can two individuals contribute different allele combinations to the same pool?

words.definition: One of two or more DNA-sequence versions at a gene or locus.

structure.text: Allele is the noun; allelic is its adjective, referring to a sequence version at a locus.

words.whatItDoes: Counting each copy allows allele frequencies to be calculated.
words.commonConfusion: A dominant allele need not be the most frequent.
words.retrievalPrompt: How many A copies do AA and Aa individuals each contribute?

words.definition: The allele combination an organism or cell carries at one or more loci.

structure.text: Genotype names allele constitution; genotypic is the adjective.

words.whatItDoes: Genotype counts determine how many copies of each allele are present.
words.commonConfusion: A phenotype may correspond to more than one genotype.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why can a dominant phenotype hide two genotypes?

words.definition: The frequency assigned to one of two alleles in a Hardy-Weinberg model.

structure.text: An italic mathematical symbol defined by the model, not an allele's name.

words.whatItDoes: It records the fraction of copies assigned to one allele.
words.commonConfusion: p is not automatically the proportion showing a dominant phenotype.
words.retrievalPrompt: What denominator belongs in a calculation of p?

words.definition: The frequency assigned to the second of two alleles in a Hardy-Weinberg model, where p + q = 1.

structure.text: A mathematical symbol for the other allele frequency in a two-allele model.

words.whatItDoes: With two alleles, it is one minus p.
words.commonConfusion: q squared, not q, is the expected recessive homozygote frequency.
words.retrievalPrompt: If p is 0.7, what is q and why?

words.definition: The Hardy–Weinberg expected frequency of AA, equal to p × p; p is the frequency of allele A, not an allele name.

structure.text: Read p-squared: the exponent means p multiplied by p.

words.whatItDoes: It predicts the homozygote frequency under random allele union.
words.commonConfusion: It is not the observed AA count unless multiplied by population size and interpreted appropriately.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why does multiplying p by p represent two copies of the same allele?

words.definition: The Hardy-Weinberg expected frequency of heterozygotes when two alleles have frequencies p and q.

structure.text: Read two-p-q: twice the product of p and q.

words.whatItDoes: It combines the two parental allele-origin arrangements producing heterozygotes.
words.commonConfusion: The two arrangements are not two different heterozygote genotypes.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why is there a factor of two?

words.definition: The Hardy–Weinberg expected frequency of aa, equal to q × q; q is the frequency of allele a, not an allele name.

structure.text: Read q-squared, the product q times q.

words.whatItDoes: It predicts the second homozygote class under the model.
words.commonConfusion: Taking q squared as q overestimates or misstates allele frequency.
words.retrievalPrompt: If recessive homozygotes are 0.09 under equilibrium, what is q?

words.definition: A model condition in which random sampling has a relatively small effect on allele frequencies; it is an approximation, not a fixed universal head count.

structure.text: Large modifies population relative to the importance of random sampling, not a universal numerical cutoff.

words.whatItDoes: Large breeding populations reduce random allele-frequency fluctuations.
words.commonConfusion: A large census may conceal a small breeding population.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why might a population with many juveniles still experience appreciable drift?

words.definition: Mating in which genotype at the focal locus does not affect partner choice or gamete union.

structure.text: Random modifies mating with respect to the locus being modelled.

words.whatItDoes: It supports the genotype proportions expected from allele frequencies.
words.commonConfusion: Random mating alone does not prevent migration or selection.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why can nonrandom mating alter genotype proportions without immediately changing allele frequencies?

words.definition: An equilibrium assumption that no allele copies enter or leave through movement of reproducing individuals or gametes.

structure.text: No negates migration, movement into or out of the defined population.

words.whatItDoes: Absence of migrants prevents this route of allele entry or loss.
words.commonConfusion: Migration only changes frequencies if its genetic contribution changes allele proportions.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why must the population boundary be specified?

words.definition: An equilibrium assumption that no new allele changes affect the locus over the modelled interval.

structure.text: No negates mutation, a change in DNA sequence.

words.whatItDoes: It excludes creation or conversion of alleles from the model.
words.commonConfusion: Mutation-free is an assumption, not a claim that real DNA never changes.
words.retrievalPrompt: What part of an allele-frequency model does mutation introduce?

words.definition: An equilibrium assumption that the compared genotypes do not differ in survival or reproductive contribution.

structure.text: No negates selection, differential reproductive contribution.

words.whatItDoes: It assumes genotype does not cause different successful contributions to the next generation.
words.commonConfusion: Equal survival alone does not establish equal reproduction.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why must reproductive success also be considered?

words.definition: The specified phenotype expressed by a homozygous recessive genotype in a complete-dominance model.

structure.text: Phenotype names the observed trait; recessive specifies its expression relationship.

words.whatItDoes: Under the simple fully penetrant model it identifies recessive homozygotes.
words.commonConfusion: Incomplete penetrance or a different inheritance model breaks that inference.
words.retrievalPrompt: What assumptions let a phenotype count estimate q squared?

words.definition: A value which, multiplied by itself, gives the original number; q is the nonnegative square root of q².

structure.text: Root names the inverse operation to squaring; take the nonnegative root for a frequency.

words.whatItDoes: It converts an equilibrium homozygote proportion to its allele frequency.
words.commonConfusion: The method is conditional on the genetic model, not a universal operation on phenotype counts.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why is the negative square root inappropriate for allele frequency?

words.definition: An individual or cell carrying two different alleles at a locus in the diploid model.

structure.text: Hetero- means different; the noun names an individual carrying different alleles at the locus.

words.whatItDoes: It contributes one copy of each allele in a two-allele count.
words.commonConfusion: A heterozygote is not a third allele.
words.retrievalPrompt: How does one heterozygote enter both allele tallies?

words.definition: The frequencies of mutually exclusive categories that together cover the whole population or gene pool must add to one.

structure.text: Sum indicates addition; frequency identifies proportions using compatible denominators.

words.whatItDoes: The complete mutually exclusive allele classes sum to one.
words.commonConfusion: Allele and genotype frequencies are different partitions and should not be mixed in one sum.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why does p plus q equal one only for the specified two-allele inventory?

words.definition: Actually recorded in the specified dataset, rather than predicted by a model.

structure.text: The past-participle adjective identifies recorded data rather than a prediction.

words.whatItDoes: Observed counts provide the data against which a model is compared.
words.commonConfusion: Observed does not mean measured without error.
words.retrievalPrompt: What observation would you collect to test predicted genotype proportions?

words.definition: Predicted under a stated model and its assumptions.

structure.text: The adjective identifies a model-derived value rather than a guaranteed outcome.

words.whatItDoes: Expected frequencies provide a comparison for the actual sample.
words.commonConfusion: A small mismatch alone does not prove selection.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why can a finite sample differ from expected counts?

words.definition: A selected subset of observations used to investigate a larger population or process.

structure.text: Sample names a subset; sampled is the participle.

words.whatItDoes: It makes estimation possible without measuring every member.
words.commonConfusion: A convenient sample may not represent the population.
words.retrievalPrompt: How could sampling one family distort an allele estimate?

words.definition: A model state in which the relevant population quantities remain stable under specified conditions.

structure.text: A condition noun; equilibrium frequencies remain stable under the stated assumptions.

words.whatItDoes: It provides a null model for allele stability and genotype proportions.
words.commonConfusion: Equilibrium does not mean individual organisms stop changing.
words.retrievalPrompt: What remains stable in Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium?

words.definition: A change in DNA sequence that can create a new allele; its contribution to a breeding gene pool depends on transmission through reproduction.

structure.text: Mutation is the change noun; mutational is the adjective.

words.whatItDoes: Sequence changes introduce new alleles or convert existing ones.
words.commonConfusion: Mutations do not arise because an organism needs a particular adaptation.
words.retrievalPrompt: How can mutation supply variation before a new pressure appears?

words.definition: Differences among organisms arising from genetic recombination, mutation, development, and environmental context.

structure.text: Variation names differences; variable is the related adjective.

words.whatItDoes: Inherited differences provide alternative phenotypes on which selection can act.
words.commonConfusion: Not all variation is inherited.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why does selection require relevant heritable variation?

words.definition: Differential reproductive contribution caused by heritable phenotypic differences in an environment.

structure.text: Selection names differential success; natural distinguishes the context from selective breeding.

words.whatItDoes: Heritable variants associated with reproductive success become differently represented.
words.commonConfusion: Individuals do not evolve a needed allele by trying.
words.retrievalPrompt: How can a pre-existing resistance allele increase after treatment?

words.definition: Relative reproductive contribution to future generations in a particular environment.

structure.text: Relative makes fitness comparative; fitness here concerns reproductive contribution.

words.whatItDoes: Comparing successful descendants links phenotype to allele-frequency change.
words.commonConfusion: Physical strength is not the definition of evolutionary fitness.
words.retrievalPrompt: Can a less strong organism have higher fitness in a particular environment?

words.definition: Random allele-frequency change caused by finite sampling across generations.

structure.text: Drift is a random-change metaphor; genetic identifies allele-frequency change.

words.whatItDoes: Finite sampling of reproducing copies shifts frequencies by chance.
words.commonConfusion: Drift is not directional improvement.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why is chance more influential in a small breeding population?

words.definition: Genetic drift caused by a sharp population reduction that leaves an unrepresentative gene pool.

structure.text: A narrow-neck metaphor for a sharp population reduction.

words.whatItDoes: The survivors carry a chance subset of earlier genetic variation.
words.commonConfusion: Recovery in numbers does not automatically restore lost alleles.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why can a recovered population retain reduced diversity?

words.definition: Genetic drift when a new population begins from a small, unrepresentative group.

structure.text: Founder identifies colonists; effect names the genetic consequence of their small starting sample.

words.whatItDoes: New populations can begin with unusual allele frequencies.
words.commonConfusion: Founders need not be better adapted than the source population.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why can a rare source allele become common in a new colony?

words.definition: Transfer of alleles among populations when migrants or their gametes reproduce.

structure.text: Flow is movement; gene identifies the transferred genetic contribution.

words.whatItDoes: Successful migrants or gametes introduce allele copies across population boundaries.
words.commonConfusion: Movement without reproduction need not contribute gene flow.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why might a visiting animal produce no gene flow?

words.definition: Movement into or out of a population; it produces gene flow when it changes the breeding gene pool.

structure.text: Migration is movement; immigration and emigration specify direction relative to a boundary.

words.whatItDoes: Movement changes counts and potentially the gene pool.
words.commonConfusion: The same movement is immigration for one population and emigration for another.
words.retrievalPrompt: How would you classify one animal's move in the source and destination populations?

words.definition: Mating in which pairings are not independent of the relevant traits or genotypes; it can change genotype proportions without initially changing allele frequencies.

structure.text: Non- negates random with respect to the traits or loci in question.

words.whatItDoes: Mate associations can change genotype proportions.
words.commonConfusion: A change in heterozygosity is not necessarily an immediate allele-frequency change.
words.retrievalPrompt: How can mating among relatives alter homozygosity?

words.definition: The capacity of a bacterial lineage to persist under an antibiotic exposure that inhibits susceptible lineages.

structure.text: Resistance is reduced susceptibility; antibiotic identifies the agent acting on bacteria.

words.whatItDoes: Resistant variants can leave more descendants during treatment.
words.commonConfusion: A patient does not acquire the bacterial resistance genotype.
words.retrievalPrompt: Which population is evolving when antibiotic resistance increases?

words.definition: The capacity of a plant lineage to survive a herbicide exposure that inhibits susceptible lineages.

structure.text: Resistance names reduced susceptibility; herbicide identifies the weed-control agent.

words.whatItDoes: Resistant plant variants can reproduce after susceptible plants are removed.
words.commonConfusion: The chemical need not create the particular useful mutation.
words.retrievalPrompt: How could resistance exist before herbicide application?

words.definition: An environmental condition associated with differences in survival or reproductive success among heritable variants.

structure.text: Pressure is a causal metaphor for conditions affecting relative reproductive success.

words.whatItDoes: It changes which existing variants tend to contribute descendants.
words.commonConfusion: A pressure does not specify the mutation that will appear.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why might the same trait be beneficial in one environment but costly in another?

words.definition: An independent repetition or sample under a defined condition used to assess variation and reliability.

structure.text: Replicate is a repeat noun or verb; replication here means repeated experimental units.

words.whatItDoes: Independent repeats reveal variation in outcomes.
words.commonConfusion: Repeated readings from one unit are not always independent replicates.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why compare several independently treated populations?

words.definition: A comparison condition or regulated variable used to make an investigation interpretable.

structure.text: Control names a comparison condition, not the act of forcing a desired result.

words.whatItDoes: A suitable comparison helps isolate the tested factor.
words.commonConfusion: A control cannot remove every possible source of bias.
words.retrievalPrompt: What should differ between treatment and control populations?

words.definition: Measurements of a specified quantity at multiple stated times.

structure.text: Series means ordered observations; time specifies the ordering variable.

words.whatItDoes: Repeated measurements show trajectories rather than only endpoints.
words.commonConfusion: Successive observations are not automatically independent.
words.retrievalPrompt: What can several time points show that a before-and-after pair cannot?

words.definition: Another mechanism that could account for the observations and should be tested or qualified.

structure.text: Alternative identifies another account of the same observation.

words.whatItDoes: Comparing predictions helps distinguish selection, drift and migration.
words.commonConfusion: A plausible account is not automatically supported by the available data.
words.retrievalPrompt: What additional evidence could separate drift from selection?

words.definition: The number of individuals, N, inside a defined population boundary.

structure.text: Size is the number of organisms, not their body dimensions.

words.whatItDoes: It is the starting quantity for balance and density calculations.
words.commonConfusion: Size and density are not interchangeable without area or volume.
words.retrievalPrompt: Can two populations have equal sizes but different densities?

words.definition: The two-dimensional extent of a region, measured in square units.

structure.text: Area measures a two-dimensional extent, usually with squared units.

words.whatItDoes: Dividing count by area gives areal density.
words.commonConfusion: Area is not volume or transect length.
words.retrievalPrompt: What units result from dividing 80 organisms by 20 square metres?

words.definition: The number of individuals per unit area or volume.

structure.text: Density names number per stated space; population density specifies organisms rather than mass.

words.whatItDoes: It standardizes counts across differently sized study areas.
words.commonConfusion: Uniform average density does not prove uniform distribution.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why can equal densities conceal different clustering?

words.definition: The spatial pattern of individuals, commonly described as clumped, uniform, or approximately random at a stated scale.

structure.text: Distribution describes spatial arrangement; distributed is the participle.

words.whatItDoes: It distinguishes clumped, random and uniform patterns.
words.commonConfusion: Distribution is not simply total number.
words.retrievalPrompt: How might patchy resources create clumping?

words.definition: A defined sampling area used to count or measure organisms in a habitat.

structure.text: A whole sampling-frame name; quadrats is plural.

words.whatItDoes: Counts in known-area samples can estimate density and abundance.
words.commonConfusion: One conveniently placed frame may be biased.
words.retrievalPrompt: How would you choose quadrat locations to reduce bias?

words.definition: A defined line or strip along which observations are collected across a habitat.

structure.text: A whole sampling-line or belt name; transects is plural.

words.whatItDoes: Observations along a defined path reveal spatial change.
words.commonConfusion: A line transect does not automatically sample all habitats equally.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why might a shore-to-inland transect be informative?

words.definition: A sampling method that estimates population size from marked individuals later recaptured in a second sample.

structure.text: The hyphen joins the two stages: marking and later recapturing.

words.whatItDoes: The recaptured marked fraction estimates the initial marked fraction of the population.
words.commonConfusion: Marks lost or unequal capture probability can bias the estimate.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why must marked individuals mix before recapture?

words.definition: A sample selected in a way that supports inference to the intended population without known systematic bias.

structure.text: Representative qualifies how well the sample reflects relevant population variation.

words.whatItDoes: Coverage of habitat and groups supports generalization.
words.commonConfusion: Large size alone does not guarantee representativeness.
words.retrievalPrompt: How could a large roadside sample still be biased?

words.definition: Births adding individuals to a population during a stated interval.

structure.text: Natality names births; natal is the birth-related adjective.

words.whatItDoes: Births add individuals to population balance.
words.commonConfusion: Birth count and birth rate require different units.
words.retrievalPrompt: What must you add to a birth count to report a rate?

words.definition: Deaths removing individuals from a population during a stated interval.

structure.text: Mortality names deaths; mortal is the related adjective.

words.whatItDoes: Deaths subtract individuals from population balance.
words.commonConfusion: Mortality rate is not necessarily the lifetime chance of dying.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why must a mortality rate include a time interval?

words.definition: Movement into a population that adds individuals to its count.

structure.text: Immigration specifies inward movement relative to the population boundary.

words.whatItDoes: Arrivals add individuals to an open population.
words.commonConfusion: Immigration is not birth.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why must arrivals be counted separately from offspring born locally?

words.definition: Movement out of a population that removes individuals from its count.

structure.text: Emigration specifies outward movement relative to the population boundary.

words.whatItDoes: Departures subtract individuals even if they remain alive.
words.commonConfusion: Emigration is not mortality.
words.retrievalPrompt: How could local numbers fall without deaths?

words.definition: A population whose size or gene pool can change through immigration and emigration as well as local births/deaths.

structure.text: Open modifies population to allow exchange across its boundary.

words.whatItDoes: Births, deaths, immigration and emigration all enter its balance.
words.commonConfusion: Open does not mean unlimited resources.
words.retrievalPrompt: Which balance terms can explain a local increase?

words.definition: A model population with no immigration or emigration during the stated interval.

structure.text: Closed specifies the no-migration assumption for the stated interval.

words.whatItDoes: Only births and deaths change its size in the simple balance.
words.commonConfusion: Closed does not mean no reproduction or death.
words.retrievalPrompt: When might treating a population as closed be a poor assumption?

words.definition: Change in population size divided by elapsed time, such as individuals per day.

structure.text: Rate means change per time; growth can be positive or negative.

words.whatItDoes: Net change divided by elapsed time gives an absolute rate.
words.commonConfusion: A negative growth rate is decline, not an impossible value.
words.retrievalPrompt: What is the rate when 100 individuals become 80 in two years?

words.definition: In this curriculum, population change divided by the initial population over a stated interval; a time-normalized rate must be labelled separately.

structure.text: Per capita means per individual; rate also requires a time basis.

words.whatItDoes: Dividing absolute change rate by the reference size enables proportional comparisons.
words.commonConfusion: The denominator and interval must be stated; it is not the raw change count.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why can a small population have a higher per-capita rate despite a smaller absolute increase?

words.definition: The elapsed duration between two defined observations.

structure.text: Interval is the elapsed span between endpoints, not the final date alone.

words.whatItDoes: It converts changes into comparable rates.
words.commonConfusion: Mixing monthly and yearly rates without conversion is invalid.
words.retrievalPrompt: How would you compare a monthly change with a yearly change?

words.definition: A population's capacity to increase under favourable conditions, before specified environmental limits reduce realized growth.

structure.text: Biotic refers to living organisms; potential denotes a capacity under favourable conditions.

words.whatItDoes: Reproductive capacity sets a possible growth tendency.
words.commonConfusion: Potential is not the growth actually observed under constraints.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why might actual growth be far below reproductive potential?

words.definition: The combined limiting factors and losses that reduce realized population increase.

structure.text: Resistance is the limiting effect; environmental identifies its source.

words.whatItDoes: Resource limits and adverse conditions reduce realized growth.
words.commonConfusion: It is not one fixed force identical in every habitat.
words.retrievalPrompt: Which conditions could reduce a population's realized growth?

words.definition: The population size an environment can sustain over time under stated conditions.

structure.text: Capacity means supportable level; carrying is an ecological metaphor.

words.whatItDoes: Resource and interaction conditions constrain long-term support.
words.commonConfusion: K is not permanently fixed or a rigid ceiling never exceeded.
words.retrievalPrompt: How could a drought change carrying capacity?

words.definition: The increasing population-size curve associated with exponential growth under stated favourable conditions.

structure.text: J names the plotted shape; curve refers to population size against time.

words.whatItDoes: An exponential model can produce an accelerating J-shaped trajectory.
words.commonConfusion: The shape alone does not prove resources are unlimited.
words.retrievalPrompt: What assumptions support an exponential projection?

words.definition: The sigmoidal population-size curve associated with a simple logistic model approaching its carrying capacity.

structure.text: S names the sigmoid shape of a population-versus-time graph.

words.whatItDoes: Logistic growth slows as the population approaches its modelled capacity.
words.commonConfusion: Real populations need not follow a smooth S trajectory.
words.retrievalPrompt: Where is logistic growth slowing and why?

words.definition: A relationship in which an effect or per-capita rate changes as population density changes.

structure.text: Dependence identifies an effect that changes with density.

words.whatItDoes: Crowding can strengthen competition or transmission.
words.commonConfusion: Not every factor affecting a population is density-dependent.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why can infection spread more readily as contact rates increase?

words.definition: Describes an effect that is not systematically related to population density over the observed range.

structure.text: Independence refers to the factor's effect not depending on population density in the model.

words.whatItDoes: Some physical disturbances affect populations regardless of crowding.
words.commonConfusion: It does not mean every individual is affected identically.
words.retrievalPrompt: How can a freeze act independently of crowding?

words.definition: A temporary rise of population size above the environment’s current carrying capacity.

structure.text: Over- indicates beyond; shoot is a trajectory metaphor here.

words.whatItDoes: Population size can temporarily exceed supportable conditions.
words.commonConfusion: Overshoot does not establish a new sustainable capacity.
words.retrievalPrompt: How can delayed feedback produce overshoot?

words.definition: A delay between a change in conditions and the resulting population response.

structure.text: Lag means delay; time identifies its duration.

words.whatItDoes: Delayed responses can sustain growth after conditions begin to deteriorate.
words.commonConfusion: A delayed response is not necessarily no response.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why might births continue after resources fall?

words.definition: A simplified life-history tendency toward earlier reproduction and many offspring under some changing or short-lived conditions.

structure.text: r is a model growth parameter; selected is the historical strategy label.

words.whatItDoes: The label summarizes traits associated with rapid reproduction under some conditions.
words.commonConfusion: It is a continuum shorthand, not two rigid species boxes.
words.retrievalPrompt: Which traits could favour rapid colonization after disturbance?

words.definition: A simplified life-history tendency toward slower reproduction and greater investment per offspring under some crowded or stable conditions.

structure.text: K is the carrying-capacity symbol; selected is the historical strategy label.

words.whatItDoes: The label summarizes traits associated with persistent competitive environments.
words.commonConfusion: It does not mean a species always lives exactly at K.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why are real life histories more varied than two labels?

words.definition: Potential reproductive output over a stated interval, distinguished from offspring that actually survive.

structure.text: Fecundity is reproductive-output capacity; fecund is the adjective.

words.whatItDoes: Potential offspring output contributes to life-history comparisons.
words.commonConfusion: High egg production is not the same as high offspring survival.
words.retrievalPrompt: How can high fecundity coexist with low recruitment?

words.definition: Resources or care directed toward offspring that can affect their survival and a parent's other reproductive opportunities.

structure.text: Investment is resource allocation; parental identifies allocation by parents to offspring.

words.whatItDoes: Care can improve offspring survival while limiting other reproductive opportunities.
words.commonConfusion: More care per offspring does not always mean more total offspring.
words.retrievalPrompt: What trade-off can occur between offspring number and care?

words.definition: An interaction in which one organism captures and consumes another organism.

structure.text: Predation is the interaction noun; predator is the consumer and prey the organism consumed.

words.whatItDoes: Consumption links survival and energy transfer between populations.
words.commonConfusion: Predation is not identical to parasitism.
words.retrievalPrompt: How could predator removal affect a prey population?

words.definition: A relationship in which a consumer obtains matter/energy from a producer, potentially changing both populations.

structure.text: The hyphen links trophic roles: production of organic matter and its consumption.

words.whatItDoes: Feeding transfers matter and some chemical energy to consumers.
words.commonConfusion: Consumers do not receive all producer energy.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why is consumer production smaller than the energy originally fixed?

words.definition: An interaction in which both participants receive a net measured benefit under stated conditions.

structure.text: A whole interaction name; mutualistic is the adjective.

words.whatItDoes: Both partners obtain benefits in the specified context.
words.commonConfusion: The relationship need not be equally beneficial or obligatory.
words.retrievalPrompt: What evidence would show benefits to both partners?

words.definition: An interaction in which one participant benefits and no effect on the other is detected.

structure.text: A whole interaction name; commensal is the associated noun or adjective.

words.whatItDoes: One partner benefits with no detectable effect on the other in the stated context.
words.commonConfusion: Failure to measure an effect is not proof no effect is possible.
words.retrievalPrompt: How would you test the supposedly unaffected partner?

words.definition: An interaction in which a parasite benefits while reducing host fitness.

structure.text: Parasitism names the relationship; parasite names the benefiting organism.

words.whatItDoes: A parasite gains resources while reducing host performance.
words.commonConfusion: A parasite does not always kill its host immediately.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why can host survival be compatible with parasite harm?

words.definition: Competition among members of the same species for limited resources.

structure.text: Intra- means within; specific refers to species membership.

words.whatItDoes: Members of the same species compete for limiting resources.
words.commonConfusion: Competition requires a limiting shared resource, not mere co-occurrence.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why can similar needs intensify within-species competition?

words.definition: Competition between members of different species for limited resources.

structure.text: Inter- means between; specific identifies different species.

words.whatItDoes: Overlapping resource use can reduce performance of one or both species.
words.commonConfusion: Different species sharing a site are not automatically competitors.
words.retrievalPrompt: What evidence would establish competition rather than simple overlap?

words.definition: Resemblance that affects another organism's response, such as a predator avoiding a look-alike prey.

structure.text: Mimicry is resemblance that changes another organism's response; mimic is the resembling organism.

words.whatItDoes: Resemblance can reduce attack or improve access to resources.
words.commonConfusion: Not every visual similarity is a demonstrated adaptation.
words.retrievalPrompt: How could predator responses support a mimicry explanation?

words.definition: Colour or pattern that can reduce detection or attack under particular environmental conditions.

structure.text: Coloration is appearance; protective specifies the proposed survival function.

words.whatItDoes: Concealment or warning signals can change predator encounters.
words.commonConfusion: Bright coloration is not always camouflage.
words.retrievalPrompt: How would you distinguish concealment from warning coloration?

words.definition: A biologically produced substance that can harm another organism under specified exposure conditions.

structure.text: Toxin names a biologically produced harmful substance; toxic is broader as an adjective.

words.whatItDoes: Chemical defences can reduce consumption or harm competitors.
words.commonConfusion: A toxin's effect depends on dose and susceptibility.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why might a defence deter one consumer but not another?

words.definition: An organism's actions or responses, which can influence survival, interactions or reproduction.

structure.text: Behaviour names an organism's actions; behavioural is the adjective.

words.whatItDoes: Actions change encounters, resource acquisition and reproductive success.
words.commonConfusion: Behaviour can reflect both inherited tendencies and experience.
words.retrievalPrompt: How could timing of activity reduce predation?

words.definition: A time difference between changes in prey abundance and a predator population's response.

structure.text: Lag names a delay; predator-prey specifies the two population trajectories.

words.whatItDoes: Predator numbers may respond after prey availability changes.
words.commonConfusion: Lagged correlation alone does not prove a simple two-species mechanism.
words.retrievalPrompt: What other factors could shift the timing of predator peaks?

words.definition: A pattern in which variables change together; it does not by itself establish a causal mechanism.

structure.text: Correlation names covariation; correlated does not mean causally linked.

words.whatItDoes: It identifies a pattern that may motivate a mechanism test.
words.commonConfusion: A common third factor can produce correlation.
words.retrievalPrompt: What evidence beyond paired graphs would support causation?

words.definition: The connected biological steps through which an effect occurs.

structure.text: Mechanism names the sequence of causal steps, not simply a repeated pattern.

words.whatItDoes: It connects a changed condition to a biological outcome.
words.commonConfusion: Restating the outcome does not explain how it occurs.
words.retrievalPrompt: What intermediate process would you measure to test your explanation?

words.definition: Community development beginning where developed soil and substantial terrestrial biological legacies are absent.

structure.text: Primary identifies development where established soil is absent; succession names community change.

words.whatItDoes: Colonization and substrate alteration enable later communities.
words.commonConfusion: Primary does not mean the first event a researcher happened to observe.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why can soil development constrain early colonists?

words.definition: Community development after disturbance where soil or other biological legacies remain.

structure.text: Secondary specifies recovery where soil or biological legacies remain.

words.whatItDoes: Surviving soil, seeds and organisms influence recovery.
words.commonConfusion: Secondary succession is not necessarily a repeat of the exact former community.
words.retrievalPrompt: How can retained soil accelerate some recovery processes?

words.definition: A developing mixture of mineral particles, organic material, organisms, air and water that supports many terrestrial communities.

structure.text: Soil is a material noun for a biologically active mixture, not only rock particles.

words.whatItDoes: It stores water and nutrients and supports organisms.
words.commonConfusion: Bare mineral substrate is not automatically developed soil.
words.retrievalPrompt: Which components make soil important for later colonists?

words.definition: Populations of different species living and interacting in an area.

structure.text: Community is the multi-species assemblage noun; community-level differs from population-level.

words.whatItDoes: Interactions among species influence composition and succession.
words.commonConfusion: A community is not one species or the full abiotic ecosystem.
words.retrievalPrompt: How does community composition differ from population size?

words.definition: A relatively persistent late-successional community under specified conditions, not an inevitable or permanently unchanging endpoint.

structure.text: Climax is the historical endpoint metaphor; community names the assemblage.

words.whatItDoes: It describes a relatively persistent state under particular conditions.
words.commonConfusion: Succession is not guaranteed to reach one permanent endpoint.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why can disturbance or climate change invalidate a fixed endpoint?

words.definition: A measured feature used to evaluate a condition or change, with its reliability and limitations stated.

structure.text: Indicator names a measured sign of a condition; it need not be its direct cause.

words.whatItDoes: A species or metric can help track environmental change.
words.commonConfusion: One indicator cannot fully describe ecosystem condition.
words.retrievalPrompt: What makes an indicator informative and what limits it?

words.definition: Repeated observation using a consistent method to detect change and evaluate a prediction or intervention.

structure.text: Monitoring is repeated observation using a consistent method.

words.whatItDoes: It detects changes over time and supports management revision.
words.commonConfusion: A one-time survey alone is not a time trend.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why preserve methods when comparing yearly counts?

words.definition: A transparent description of limits in measurement, sampling, models, evidence, or prediction.

structure.text: Un- negates certainty; the noun identifies limits in precision or inference.

words.whatItDoes: Acknowledging uncertainty constrains the strength of conclusions.
words.commonConfusion: Uncertainty does not mean all explanations are equally plausible.
words.retrievalPrompt: Which uncertainty comes from sampling and which from model assumptions?

words.definition: A way of evaluating an issue shaped by evidence, values, experience or responsibilities.

structure.text: Perspective names a standpoint or framing of a question.

words.whatItDoes: Different priorities can affect which outcomes are investigated or valued.
words.commonConfusion: A value priority does not change a measured count by itself.
words.retrievalPrompt: How can two stakeholders agree on evidence but prefer different actions?

words.definition: A reasoned change to a prediction, explanation or plan after considering evidence or feedback.

structure.text: Re- indicates doing again; revision is a reasoned change to an account or plan.

words.whatItDoes: New evidence can justify updating predictions or management.
words.commonConfusion: Revision is not arbitrary alteration to protect a preferred conclusion.
words.retrievalPrompt: What new result would make you revise your explanation?

words.definition: Differences in reproductive contribution associated with success in obtaining mates or fertilizations; distinguish this from nonrandom pairing alone.

structure.text: Sexual qualifies selection through differences in mating or fertilization success.

words.whatItDoes: Traits can spread by increasing reproductive access despite survival costs.
words.commonConfusion: It is not limited to male competition or conscious choice.
words.retrievalPrompt: How could a conspicuous display increase reproduction but increase predation?

words.definition: The proportion of an initial group that remains alive at successive ages.

structure.text: Survivorship names survival across ages; survivor names an individual remaining alive.

words.whatItDoes: Age-specific survival describes a life-history pattern.
words.commonConfusion: Survivorship is not the same as population growth.
words.retrievalPrompt: How can two species have different survivorship but similar total population change?

words.definition: A group defined by a shared starting interval or event and followed through time.

structure.text: A whole grouping noun for individuals sharing a starting event or interval.

words.whatItDoes: Following a cohort separates age-related change from mixed-age counts.
words.commonConfusion: A cross-section of all ages is not a single birth cohort.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why follow individuals born in the same period?

words.definition: An idealized survival pattern with relatively low early mortality and most losses later in life.

structure.text: Roman I labels a curve class, not a fitness rank.

words.whatItDoes: Most survive early and middle life before mortality rises later.
words.commonConfusion: The pattern is a generalization, not immunity to early death.
words.retrievalPrompt: Where does a Type I curve decline most steeply?

words.definition: An idealized survival pattern with approximately constant per-capita mortality risk across ages.

structure.text: Roman II labels a curve class; survivorship identifies the age-survival relationship.

words.whatItDoes: An approximately constant mortality risk produces a steady decline on a logarithmic survivor axis.
words.commonConfusion: A straight line depends on the graph's axis scale.
words.retrievalPrompt: Why must you inspect the vertical scale before comparing curves?

words.definition: An idealized survival pattern with high early mortality and greater subsequent survival among those passing the early stages.

structure.text: Roman III labels a curve class, not a third developmental stage.

words.whatItDoes: High early mortality leaves relatively few longer-lived survivors.
words.commonConfusion: Producing many offspring does not ensure many survive.
words.retrievalPrompt: How can high early mortality be compatible with persistent populations?
